newsitem.title: CHINA: China official says 35 killed in plane crash.
newsitem.headline: China official says 35 killed in plane crash.

text.p: At least 35 people were killed in China's first big aviation disaster for almost three years when a Boeing 737 crashed while landing in the southern city of Shenzhen, an official said on Friday.

China Southern Airlines flight CZ3456 from the southwestern city of Chongqing crashed during a thunderstorm at the new Huangtian airport serving Shenzhen, a prosperous city on the Chinese border with Hong Kong, local officials said.
The cause of the crash is still under investigation. The aircraft, carrying 65 passengers and nine crew, broke up and burst into flames, officials said.
A Shenzhen city government official said 35 people were killed when the three-year-old 737-300 crashed and burned at around 9.30 p.m. (1330 GMT) on Thursday night.
It was unclear if any of the 33 passengers killed in the crash were foreigners, the official said by telephone. The two others killed were crew members.
Earlier, a Boeing spokesman in Beijing said about 30 people had died.
"There was a Thai tour group. There were no Europeans or Americans," the city government official said.
Thirty-five people were rushed to hospital, including three Thais, one Taiwanese and one Hong Kong resident, the official said.
The conditions of the remaining four were not known.
The ill-fated flight had originally been scheduled to land at Shenzhen's international airport but had been diverted because of the heavy rain.
"It's pretty chaotic out there," the Boeing spokesman said.
The official Xinhua news agency described casualties as heavy, but gave no death toll.
"The fuselage of the airliner was broken," Xinhua said. "The cause of the accident is still under investigation."
A group of about 25 Thai tourists were aboard the aircraft, an airline spokesman said.
Staff at one Shenzhen hospital said two middle-aged Thai men had been injured but that their condition was not serious.
The Hong Kong Standard quoted a spokesman for Shenzhen's People's Hospital as saying one Thai woman was admitted with multiple fractures of her knees, ribs and head, but her condition was stable.

"The attitude of the plane during landing was wrong," one airline official said by telephone after the crash, in what appeared to be a reference to the positioning and angle of the plane during landing.
The crash occurred as Shenzhen was being pelted with rain from a severe thunderstorm.
The airliner's co-pilot was among those killed by the impact or by the blaze that tore through the aircraft immediately afterwards, another official said.

The disaster was the first to hit China Southern since another of its fleet of about 35 Boeing 737s slammed into a hill near the scenic southern city of Guilin in November, 1992. That accident killed all 141 people aboard.

Chinese aviation officials had been celebrating almost three years without a serious accident, a record credited to improved precautions taken after a Russian-made Tupolev-154 exploded in mid-air after takeoff on a domestic flight in June, 1994.
That catastrophe killed 160 people, making it the worst reported accident in China's aviation history.

It occurred just months after the International Airline Passengers Association cited China as one of the most dangerous places in the world to fly after five aircraft crashed in 1993 and 10 airliners were hijacked to Taiwan.
In 1992, a series of accidents over a four-month period killed 276 passengers, including many foreigners.
